Mr. Speaker, I wish to report to the house in connection with the final payment for the 1960-61 wheat pool account, and advise that because of the increased volume of wheat exports it is now possible to close this account and increase the initial payment for wheat delivered during the current crop year.
As at the close of business, February 28, 1962 the board will close the accounts for the 1960-61 pool account for wheat in order that a final payment can be issued to producers. The final accounting will be completed as rapidly as possible and the issuance of final payment cheques will commence not later than April 2. This payment we hope will be completed on or before April 30, which will correspond to the time of heavy costs during seeding operations by grain farmers. Producers delivered 392,824,536 bushels of wheat into the 1960-61 pool account, and the final surplus for distribution will not be known until the accounting is completed.
Effective March 1, 1962 the initial price paid to producers who deliver wheat to the 1961-62 pool account will be increased as follows:
(1)	10 cents per bushel on all wheat other than Durum, whatever the grade, including all grades of sample and mixed wheats.
(2)	75 cents per bushel on Durum wheat grading No. 1 to No. 4 including Extra No. 4, toughs, damps and all off grades.
In respect of deliveries by producers in the 1961-62 pool account for wheat for the period August 1, 1961 to February 28, 1962, both dates inclusive, an adjustment payment will be made to producers at the rates which I have previously stated in order to raise the deliveries for this period to the new and higher price level which becomes effective March 1, 1962. The increase and the adjustment payment of 10 cents per bushel will bring the initial price of No. 1 Manitoba
northern wheat to $1.50 per bushel basis in store Fort William, Port Arthur or Vancouver. In the case of Durums, the increase and the adjustment payment of 75 cents per bushel will bring the initial price for No. 1 Canada western amber Durum to $2.50 per bushel basis in store Fort William, Port Arthur or Vancouver.
The adjustment payment will involve a distribution of approximately $20 million. The issuance of cheques for this payment will commence around the beginning of May, following the completion of the final payment for the 1960-61 pool account, and will be completed on or before May 28, 1962.
I would also like to inform hon. members that on February 19 last the Canadian wheat board commenced the issuance of cheques on the 1961-62 acreage payment. This payment, involving approximately $42 million, will be completed not later than March 16 to the holders of wheat board delivery permits which have been issued to that date.

Mr. Speaker, I know that all in western Canada will be glad to hear that it is possible to make a larger initial payment, particularly this year because there is a shortage of cash in western Canada as a result of the poor deliveries which resulted from the lack of moisture last year. Farmers will also be interested, I know, to hear from the government very soon as to whether the first payment on the nine months' credit extended in connection with the special sales to China has been made by the China Resources Company. I believe that payment is due in a few days.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: INCREASE IN ALLOWABLE EARNINGS OF DEPENDANTS
speechtext:
I wish to bring to the attention of hon. members a change in the regulations of the unemployment insurance commission relating to the allowable earnings of dependants consequent upon the recent increase in old age pensions. Previously, under unemployment insurance dependancy regulations, dependants were permitted to have an income of up to $14 per week. The recent increases in old age pensions will have the effect of bringing the income of senior citizens across Canada to $65 per month, which brings them above the present permissible ceiling.
The commission has now approved a change in regulations bringing the allowable earnings to $20 per week, which will mean that a senior citizen can still be claimed as a dependant by a member of his family who is a claimant and1 is his sole support. The same regulation will, of course, apply to all dependants whether senior citizens or otherwise. The new regulation is effective February 1, and if any adjustments are required to cover interim cases they will be made accordingly.

Mr. Speaker, on Monday last the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria inquired concerning icebreaking facilities at North Sydney.
I have made inquiries and find that this winter the icebreakers Labrador, McDonald, Wolfe, d'Iberville and Alexander all operate from Sydney, and their task is to provide icebreaking assistance to any vessel requiring it. However, the number of icebreakers available precludes the possibility of assigning one or more to any specific port although Sydney and North Sydney have some advantage over other ports in that the icebreakers return there for fuel and stores. speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, February 21, consideration of the motion of Mr. Rodrigue Bourdages for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Late last Sunday afternoon a Montreal newspaperman called Oliver Clawson located me at a public gathering in Toronto. When I was given his phone number I thought to myself "Good lord, what have I said now about Quebec. What does he want to know?" When I got talking to him he asked what I knew about the departure from the New Democratic party of its house leader, Mr. Hazen Argue. I laughed at him and told him to roll that hoop in another direction. He insisted that a statement on Mr. Argue's defection was imminent and asked what did I think about it; had I talked it over with Mr. Argue; how was I sure this was just a gimmick of Mr. Thatcher, and how well did I really know Mr. Argue?
When I had finished the conversation I thought I had straightened Mr. Clawson out, but within a few hours my self-satisfaction was shattered. A news broadcast said that Mr. Argue, at a press conference attended by Mr. Thatcher, had announced his departure from the New Democratic party; that he had found the party was dominated by a

The Address-Mr. Fisher labour clique, and that dark and sinister things were abroad in Canada. The shock to me was overwhelming. This almost seemed like a fantasy, but it turned out that it was not a fantasy, though one part of the story was and is.
My colleagues in this party, particularly the three who joined with me in supporting this man for the party leadership, have asked me to speak in this debate about our departed colleague. It is my duty, I feel, because some of the responsibility for what happened is certainly mine. Further, this departure was accompanied by comments of its author which hinted that other members of this parliamentary party shared his views and would soon follow him. There is nothing in this; we are in, of, and for the party.
Mr. T. C. Douglas commented last Sunday over his shock and said that of course it was Mr. Argue's own business and up to his own conscience. We here, his former colleagues, take no issue with any hon. member or any citizen changing party allegiance in order to be more at home with his conscience and principles, and apparently Mr. Argue has almost found such a spiritual home, in the political sense, with the Liberal party. We wish the party well with him. Looking at it in the light of the rise to prominence of another C.C.F.'er in that party, like Mr. Thatcher, we can see how valuable a political training framework has been provided by J. S. Woodsworth, M. J. Coldwell and others. No; there is no real issue so far as we are concerned with freedom of choice about this.
Indeed, it has been my own personal view that there has been too much of a fetish about hide-bound partisanship in politics in Canada. My good friend from Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) was once a supporter of the Liberal party, as was my hon. friend from Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey). So was the Prime Minister, and I once acted as poll clerk and scrutineer for the Liberal party. It is hard for me to say that this kind of experience tainted me. So, Mr. Speaker, there are no recriminations on the right of this man to switch, or on the party he is embracing. After these remarks we shall not take up the time of the house again this session on the departure from this place of honour on the part of the hon. member for Assiniboia, but we must take up the reasons given with such cool, deliberate malignity for resigning from the party.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Order. I think the hon. member, in attributing malignancy to another hon. member, is trespassing upon the proper rules of conduct among hon. members.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I will withdraw the word "malignity", but I think it is certainly fair to say "given so coolly and deliberately for resigning from the party". Essentially these are contained in the last paragraphs of the initial statement which he made. Of course this statement has been enlarged and garnished by its author, and the tale will probably grow with each telling. However, let us look at these paragraphs:
The N.D.P. has now become the tool of a small labour clique and is effectively under their domination and control. The N.D.P. has come more and more under the control of a few labour leaders, mainly within a few large and powerful international unions.
Labouring people, as with other citizens, have a right and obligation to take part in political activity, but it is in their best interest and in the interest of democratic government, that this action be taken as individual party members and not as representatives of a controlling class bloc within the party. Class control of a national political party now acquired within the N.D.P. constitutes a dark and sinister threat to democratic government in Canada.
This challenge to freedom is real. This challenge to freedom, I shall oppose and expose.
To this task I shall devote all my strength and energy. I do this in the defence of freedom and in the interest of my country.
You will forgive the zest I put into that reading, Mr. Speaker. It was as though John Blackmore or Ross Thatcher were nudging me.
The conception of the New Democratic party received public notice in April, 1958, at the C.L.C. convention in Winnipeg, shortly after the great triumph of the Prime Minister and his party in March. As a result of that election there was a total collapse of the Social Credit party and a debacle for both the Liberal and the C.C.F. parties. Our leader, Mr. Coldwell, was defeated although he undertook to carry on outside the house for a time. Then in the summer of 1958 the C.C.F. decided to join with the C.L.C. in a new party program.
The hon. member for Assiniboia had been chosen as our house leader, and he took part in the committee that was formed to set up the New Democratic party. We had two members of our caucus on the committee that was planning the new party; one was the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) and the other was the hon. member for Assiniboia. Throughout the whole period from 1958 to 1961 this man was or could have been in on all the deliberations, most of which were held in Ottawa where he was working and living. Remember this point; throughout the whole period he was at the heart of the whole project, from 1958 to the founding convention. In all that time and at all those many

meetings the other members of this committee cannot remember a single substantial objection raised by the hon. member for Assiniboia about labour representation in the party, labour affiliation with the party or labour finances in the party. Perhaps they have forgotten. Perhaps they are not telling the truth. Perhaps they have forgotten, but I have some memories on that very question. You see, one of the greatest doubters in the C.C.F. about this whole problem happened to be me.
In three articles given such wide prominence by our ever-loving press, in a statement to an Ontario C.C.F. convention, I reviewed the possible weaknesses of labour support. Did the hon. member from Assiniboia, from 1959 to the founding convention, ever join me publicly or privately in such fears? Not once, Mr. Speaker, not once. Repeatedly he was questioned, particularly by the hon. member for Kootenay West and by me about what was going on in those planning sessions. All we got was the general answer that everything was great. Which member of the caucus at this time was stamping around the nation talking to every trade union audience available, and carrying what message? I should just like to read what the general message was:
Farmers who today constitute only some 12 per cent of the population are still a major key to political success. Almost half of the electoral polls are still classified as rural. But if the farm vote is a key to political success so is support from labour necessary if the farmer is to be a political partner in government. The working people in the factories and on the farms have every reason to unite.
The problem facing both is that the great wealth of our nation is being concentrated in the hands of fewer and fewer people.
This was the message that was carried across the country by the hon. member for Assiniboia.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Will the hon. member give the source?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Yes, the source is an article by Mr. Hazen Argue that appeared in the founding edition of the New Democratic party paper, The Commonwealth, on page 18. That was the hon. member for Assiniboia from 1958 to August 2, 1961. And his star ascended. The C.C.F. held a national convention in 1960 at Regina. The house was sitting at the time. We sent our house leader off from here with our blessing. "Seek the C.C.F. national leadership", we told him. Mr. Coldwell was retiring. We said, "Let us not have any hiatus before the founding convention. You take the leadership". He promised that he would run for the post.
The Address-Mr. Fisher
I arrived late, at the Regina convention, to find that our friend had agreed not to run and had decided to withdraw. We were going to have a hiatus. My friends in the caucus and I did not particularly like this, so we got together at that convention and we got the hon. member for Assiniboia to change his mind. I have confessed my responsibility in this. I think this is the incident that really began to put responsibility on me for what has happened. My first words must be words of congratulation to the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne for the constructive way in which they presented their points of view. I wish also to extend my Congratulations to the member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau) on his appointment as Deputy Speaker and to the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Flynn) on his appointment as Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys.
My purpose in taking part in this debate today is to express some points of view on matters which affect the people in my riding. Before dealing with specific topics, however, I cannot but comment on the desperate efforts of the Liberals to confuse the issues before us at the present time. There is no denying that we are faced with many serious problems for whose solution understanding, study and sincere effort are needed. But the government, by very active programs, has been seeking remedies for these difficulties. The Liberals, on the other hand, want to take credit for the years of prosperity in a prosperous world, and then to blame the Conservatives for economic difficulties in this country which have been brought about by world conditions and world trends.
The opposition ignores the fact that the factors which led to our present economic difficulties were ever present when a Liberal administration was in power. It is not to their credit that a world war and the Korean war provided prosperity and economic development in the absence of competition from industrial countries which had been destroyed by those wars. Nor it is our fault that the competition offered by a restored Europe and Japan has limited the prospects for our own trade expansion and seriously challenged our trade in our own markets; or has this party caused automation and other trends which have brought about changes and unemployment. The Canadian people were not prepared for these changes, and no provision was made to meet growing competitions from abroad.
I blame the Liberal party for this; they were blinded by temporary prosperity, and

did not see the warning signs. Their hindsight is more vocal than their barren foresight. It is easy during times of war to establish secondary industries fed with cost plus contracts. It is much more difficult to expand and create industries when conditions are more competitive. The Liberals floated in the ship of state on the high waters of good times without a rudder or compass. They just floated with the tide. On the other hand this government since it came into power has given assistance to every part of our economy, to every province of our nation.
I do not have time to list all that has been done to assist the farmers, the miners, the businessmen and industry, or the social benefits which have been returned to our people, but I am sure those who have received such benefits can judge how hollow are the present promises and lamentations of the Liberal party. I hasten to add, however, that although we have done a great deal to meet the problems of the day, we realize there are a great many more things to be done. We know that if our people are to enjoy the rich resources which are ours much thought, study and action must be undertaken; and because I have confidence in the leadership of our Prime Minister and the cabinet I know no effort will be spared and no suggestion ignored for the benefit of the country.
The Liberals have quoted statements indicating the attitude of people outside the country concerning Canadian development. I should like to place on the record one extract from a United States magazine entitled Business Week, issue of December 23, 1961. On the page dealing with Canada the following comment is found. After pointing out the difficulties on the Canadian horizon it said:
Lying behind Canada's improved economic outlook for 1962 are the expansionary policies adopted by the Progressive Conservative government of Prime Minister John G. Diefenbaker last June, in the wake of the forced resignation of austere nationalistic James E. Coyne as governor of the Bank of Canada.
With Coyne removed from a position in which he was able to obstruct expansionist policies, the Canadian government moved quickly to administer a strong dose of monetary and fiscal medicine to the Canadian economy. That medicine is now starting to take effect.
That is the comment of an outsider.
I wish to make a few remarks concerning trade, and particularly the common market. During September of last year I had the privilege, together with five other hon. members of this house, of attending the seventh commonwealth parliamentary conference in London, where members of legislature bodies from all parts of the commonwealth had the opportunity of discussing their mutual problems. This conference was composed of people representative of many races, cultures and

groups. All were concerned with trade and the development of their resources. All expressed great hope in the future of the commonwealth and stressed the need for mutual co-operation and assistance.
Great concern was expressed over the effect of the United Kingdom entering the European economic community, better known as the common market. All members expressed concern and pointed out the adverse effects on their economy that would flow as a result of the United Kingdom joining the European economic community, and referred to the loss of the imperial preferences established in 1932. Many would be more adversely affected in their trade than Canada, especially New Zealand, Australia, Ghana and Nigeria. Incidentally, India has based its next five year plan on the present trade arrangements with the United Kingdom and would be seriously affected.
In the United Kingdom opposition to entry into the common market cuts across party lines. Labour and Conservative members have spoken out forcibly against it. However, it is apparent that the majority of the leaders in politics and industry and in the labour movement in England feel that Great Britain must enter the European economic community for both political and economic reasons.

I urge the government to make a very careful
The Address-Mr. Morton assessment and give reasoned leadership to prepare the people of Canada for the great changes which may take place.
It should be clearly understood that under the present terms of the treaty only European countries can join the common market, as set out in article 237. It is true that there is provision for associate membership under article 3(k), but this would be only on a colonial or dependency basis. There would be no representation in assembly, council or commission as set out in article 4. Within the common market group there is to be free and unrestricted movement of capital and persons. There must be a modification of local laws to assist the functioning of the common market and, of course, there are to be no tariffs between the member countries but a common tariff against the entry of goods from outside the countries.
I turn now to a growing problem created by our changing society, the place or role of the displaced workman who may be unskilled or middle aged. This person through no fault of his own may find himself without work. I know a great deal is being done by local employment offices to assist these people, but a great deal more remains to be done. I urge the government to double its efforts and research to help these people find new roles in our Canadian society.
The proposed pension scheme and especially portable pensions, relate closely to this problem, as does the workman who retires at age 65. I think there must be an over-all new approach to these interrelated problems to provide more hope to people who are caught up in the human problems created by these changes.
Another matter which I should like to bring to the attention of the government is the problem of municipal finance. The recent brief of the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities brought to our attention the great problem of municipal finance and requested federal assistance. Although we realize that municipalities are under provincial jurisdiction, their lack of finance could hinder the basic development of our country, and the works required could give much needed employment.
The federal government has already recognized the basic needs in its housing legislation, winter works programs and more recently loans to municipalities for the construction of sewers, as well as assistance, through the Minister of Labour to vocational and technical training. The question which arises is as to the best way of giving assistance within our constitutional responsibility.
A number of suggestions have been made. They include the extension of loans for specific projects which are required in the

The Address-Mr. Morton rapid growth of our municipalities, such as loans for construction of sewers; the establishment of a municipal loan fund, with regard to which problems of administration could arise; the establishment of a provincial-municipal bank or financial corporation which could co-ordinate financing of all municipal requirements. The original capital could be obtained by dominion-provincial investment and, of course, municipal bonds could be placed on the market in a more orderly fashion. Also suggested is the establishment of the same type of institution in each province with the same function. This, of course, would be more within the spirit of the British North America Act, but questions have been raised as to whether all the provinces would be in a position to establish such institutions.
The problem is big enough and important enough, having regard to the effect on our national expansion, to warrant serious study and action by the federal government. I urge the government to study these proposals and others in order to ascertain the best possible solution.
Perhaps the house would be interested in the effect of immigration since the 1951 census on the ethnic composition of the population in Toronto, and in particular in my own riding of Davenport. This effect has been ascertained as the result of a study sponsored by the city of Toronto planning board in the summer of 1960. One of the most striking developments in the ethnic composition of the population of the city of Toronto during the period 1951 to 1960 was the decline in the percentage of people of British descent. The 1951 census showed that about 70 per cent of the population were of British descent. The 1960 figures showed that only 40 per cent of the population were of British descent.
During the nine years it is estimated that 385,500 persons moved into the metropolitan Toronto area from foreign countries. Virtually all these persons settled initially within the limits of the city of Toronto. Of the immigrants coming into the Toronto area, 33 per cent were British, 22 per cent Italian and 13 per cent German. Whereas in 1951 besides the British only Italian, Polish and German immigrants were the most numerous, by 1960 there were eight ethnic groups in addition to the British entering Canada, each numbering more than 20,000, namely Italian, German, Jewish, Ukrainian, French, Polish, Hungarian and Greek. In my riding it is estimated that the population is about 35 per cent Italian, 30 per cent British, 10 per cent Ukrainian, 10 per cent German and 10 per cent Polish. Toronto has become one of the most cosmopolitan cities in Canada.
This great inflow of human wealth which has brought a rich diversity of cultures and


customs is evident also in many other parts of this country. It has challenged our ability to bring about a reasonable integration and the development of a Canadian culture which will reflect the contribution of all the various cultures.
At this stage of our history it is most important that we develop our pride in Canada and stress national unity. If we are to develop into a great nation we must provide the opportunity for all people to have one common ideal and ambition, and at the same time retain the best of their own cultures. Political union and national pride do not necessarily prevent the growth of local cultures. It is a paradox in this changing world that while many nations are pooling their sovereignties in order to ensure peace in the world, others are seeking independence in order to satisfy national pride. Within Canada we cannot afford, by drift and indifference, to encourage separate cultures to become separate political entities. We must be big enough and understanding enough to provide a political unity which will also give scope for various cultures to grow and enrich our future Canadian culture.
I hope the government will give leadership in this integration and national growth, and that by 1967 we shall have the outward symbols of unity such as one flag and the right to amend our own constitution. We are at the crossroads of our national growth and development. We face the dislocation of new international trade movements and the threat of communist expansion. Internally we are trying to grow nationally and to bring together the different groups, cultures and economic trends. If we cannot find a modus vivendi by which to achieve this national unity, how can we expect to achieve peace in the world at large? I hope that by 1967 we can celebrate the hundredth birthday of our country by showing real unity and national understanding, thereby providing opportunity for the human and cultural development of our many groups who have one thing in common, namely the welfare of Canada taking its part as a nation in the world, seeking peace and proving that communism is wrong.

Over the years, Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition has spoken out against communist imperialism as strongly as and certainly more often than the Prime Minister. Even though he was not naive enough to consider any speech an effective weapon against communism or as Canada's greatest contribution to world peace, surely there is no question as to where the Leader of the Opposition stood and stands in that respect. I wish to place on record a portion of a speech made by the Leader of the Opposition before the United Nations general assembly on September 26, 1949:
Imperialism of the old kind is a rapidly diminishing force-a dying doctrine. The real danger today lies in the new imperialism of the post-war period. During that period only one state in the world has extended its borders and the area of its domination. That state has annexed 179,000 square miles of territory and included within its borders in the last ten years more than 21 million people. Backed by its armies, it has imposed satellite regimes on neighbouring states. It has used its great material power and resources to rivet its economic control over the peoples under its influence. Its leaders have talked freely of "liberation" and of "national sovereignty", but its agents abroad have never hesitated to proclaim their obedience to its control and their determination to serve its interest above the interests of their own governments and their own peoples.
How can there be a feeling of peace and security where an alien power insists on imposing its domination over other nations and peoples?
In another speech at the United Nations on December 1, 1949 the Leader of the Opposition had this to say:
Mr. Vyshinsky asks us to believe in the lamblike qualities of Russian revolutionary communism. Naturally we do not believe this, and we are not deceived by it.
If Mr. Vyshinsky really wishes to do something about the preservation of peace, he should try to persuade his government to pay some attention to the fear in the world of this new imperialism: to the concern which is deep and widespread about the methods which it adopts to spread its influence, and the threats to peace which are inherent in those methods.
Within the U.S.S.R. sphere of influence-the new Soviet empire-have been included many peoples

who previously had their own free governments: Finns, Estonians, Ukrainians, Latvians, Lithuanians. Poles, Rumanians.
Not all the impassioned eloquence of Mr. Vyshinsky or Mr. Manuilsky can convince us that these peoples, of their own free will, happily and confidently have entrusted their destinies and their persons to the U.S.S.R. The fact that the Soviet union government finds it necessary to cut off the inhabitants of its territories from all normal contacts with other countries and to distort and manipulate information about other peoples in order to create misunderstanding and fear is, to us, convincing evidence to the contrary.
In an address to the House of Commons on August 31, 1950 the Leader of the Opposition said:
Know your enemy is a principle taught to every soldier .. . the first characteristic of Soviet communist imperialism is that its operations are on a world wide scale. Believing, as they do, that their slave system is in inevitable opposition to the free systems of government of other people, the masters of the Kremlin survey in their calculations every part of the globe.
The second aspect of Soviet power is that while it is prepared to impose its will on other peoples by military aggression, it can also act-and does act-in other ways and through other agencies. It has at its command the weapons of conspiracy, subversion and mass agitation.
Third, we must be clear about the elements in a free society which Soviet communism uses and perverts for its own program of oppression, degradation and expansion. Our job is to play our part, a part determined by ourselves but worked out in consultation with our friends, in the collective effort of the free countries to prevent aggression, if possible by showing that it cannot succeed, or to defeat it if it occurs.

Mr. Speaker, I realize that several hon. members intend to take part in this debate and I shall, therefore, try to be as brief as possible. However, I should like to congratulate most heartily the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, the hon. members for Laval (Mr. Bourdages) and Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Browne) whose remarks were full of enthusiasm and sincerity.
I should also like to congratulate the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Flynn) on his recent appointment as Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys. His competence in both parliamentary and professional matters, his moderation and good judgment will be most useful to Canada.
I would be remiss if I did not mention the appointment of Hon. Paul Comtois to the position of lieutenant governor of the prov-

ince of Quebec. His Excellency is the very impersonation of dignity and possesses to a degree the most important qualification required to hold that high office: a genuine love for his province and his country.
Several matters for discussion are suggested to us in the speech from the throne. I intend to deal with a few of them in the course of my remarks, but I should like first of all to discuss a question of great present interest which has not been overlooked in the speech from the throne, considering that the latter does refer to measures relating to the confederative pact.
It is common knowledge that at present serious difficulties lead to misunderstanding between the two main racial groups of Canada, that is English-speaking and Frenchspeaking Canadians.
The main topic of conversations and writings these last few months has been separatism. This serious problem should not be ignored by anyone, especially the elected representatives of the Canadian people, regardless of racial origin. It is impossible for me to assess at this time all the consequences which would result if Quebec should secede from the rest of the country, but I am afraid that the bad ones would be greater than the good ones. In any case, Mr. Speaker, the problem is definitely before the Canadian nation and it calls for a solution. The public authorities, politicians, citizens throughout the country, educators worthy of their calling cannot shy from it without failing in a serious moral and civil obligation.
Those who are in favour of separatism have many grievances. Some of these may seem exaggerated to the English-speaking population, but, bearing in mind the principle of justice, most of them are perfectly legitimate. I should like to have the time to analyse each and every one of the causes which have contributed to the misunderstanding between the two racial groups, but this is impossible at the moment. I shall therefore deal only with the main one, that is, bilingualism.
In this country, Mr. Speaker, bilingualism is a one-way street. It is compulsory only for French-speaking Canadians, and I must add that this situation is extremely painful and unfair.
Before going any further in my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I want to make something clear. When you hear the French-speaking members bring up matters concerning the rights of our minority group, do not believe
The Address-Mr. Lafreniere that we wish to impose on the Anglo-Canadian majority our language, our culture and our religion. We want only that they should have their rightful place in the Canadian context.
We do not pretend that the French culture is the best in the world; we do not pretend that it is either superior or inferior to the Anglo-Saxon culture. In some matters, comparisons are undesirable. We do not have either, as some people say, a superiority complex, but we do have an equality complex.
Why should it be amazing for a nation to feel strongly about its language, its faith, its customs and its traditions? When we have children, because we see them through our love, we usually find them handsome and bright. From those points of view, they are probably not any better than the neighbour's children but we are attached to them because they are our own. The same thing goes for a people with regard to its heritage. One must understand that this can be a very deep feeling, although it does not preclude full appreciation of, and participation in the culture and institutions of another people.
This has always been our attitude regarding Anglo-Saxon culture.
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that English-speaking Canadians will not blame us because we are defending our rights when our claims are justified.
We have known for a long time that "fair play" is an essential part of the intellectual and mental discipline of Anglo-Saxons. However, I suggest that they have so far omitted to put such fair play into practice, particularly in connection with bilingualism in this country. It must be realized that at least 6 million French-speaking Canadians living in this country feel compelled to learn a second language while English-speaking Canadians, up to now at least, have shown indifference toward a second language.
Now, a hundred years after confederation, a hundred years after the convention passed between the two ethnic groups of this country to the effect that French and English should both be the official languages of Canada, we bitterly notice that we, Canadians, have undoubtedly ignored one of the main clauses in our agreement.
I will not mention any other evidence than the words of the secretary to the Canadian conference on education, Dr. Seraphin Marion, following a study that the conference was able to conduct through a donation from the Ford Foundation.

The Address-Mr. Lafreniere
This is a most interesting investigation carried out by the foundation on the teaching of the second language in Canada.
Dr. Marion writes:
It would be foolhardy to live in an illusory world and to act like the ostrich in the Canada of 1962. A whole set of events took place in 1961 and they should open the eyes of the most optimistic and bring them back to hard realities. At the present time, all Canadians must admit the following: there are major obstacles in the way of national unity-or rather the union between the two nations co-existing in our country, the English speaking Canadian nation and the French speaking Canadian nation. And unless all those concerned make vigorous efforts, we shall probably see in a short time that a difficult, and even tragic, situation has developed.
Those views, Mr. Speaker, clearly show that some serious prejudice has been done, and that someone is certainly responsible for it. In my opinion, those responsible are the various administrations which have succeeded one another since confederation, until the coming into power, in 1957, of the Conservative government.
The Prime Minister of Canada said all over the country, during the 1957 election campaign and later, that it was his intention to respect the spirit of the confederative pact, and he has kept his word.
Besides, Mr. Speaker, it is a fact that in a country with a constitution like ours, the state, the central government, must take all the required but fair measures to promote the full development of the various racial groups forming the nation.
Failure to fulfil that duty has been the awful mistake of the previous Liberal administration, which has been in power for nearly a quarter of a century and which has always turned a deaf ear to the fair claims and rights of minorities in this country.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that I would have become a separatist if the Conservative government had not given such excellent evidence of good will toward national unity, to which the Liberals so often refer but about which they have done absolutely nothing.
I am proud to be a member of the present government because it is, among other reasons, the only one that has taken concrete steps, that has achieved practical objectives in recognition of the rights of the minority I represent, in part, in this house.
The French racial group has obtained tangible results from the present government and those gains have caused no prejudice nor injustice to other Canadians.
Constructive criticism often becomes necessary, but there are times, however, when we are duty bound to express our gratitude.

I should mention at this point a particular event which took place these last few years in our national life. For the first time in history, the government has appointed as representative of the Queen a French-speaking person: His Excellency Governor General Georges Vanier.
It must be noted, as I have already pointed out, that there is in this country, out of every three Canadians, one French-speaking Canadian.
It is to the Prime Minister and to his government that we owe that great consideration. It is also to the Conservative government that we owe the installation of a simultaneous interpretation system in the House of Commons, which allows Englishspeaking Canadians and French-speaking Canadians to better understand each other.
As the representative of a constituency in which Laval University, is situated, I believe I should thank this Conservative government for having settled the problem of university grants to such great advantage. Such action is another step towards attainment of the true spirit of confederation. In this connection I should also mention that the Conservative government has increased provincial tax levies from 10 to 16 per cent, a percentage that will be raised to 20 per cent by annual increases of one per cent.
This means, Mr. Speaker, that during the few years it has been in power, this government has given the provinces twice as much as the Liberals gave them. So, in that field also, the Prime Minister kept his promise when he told us that he wished to make the spirit of the Canadian confederation a reality in this country.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I should like to move on to another subject along the same line. One of the main causes of the uneasiness which is felt throughout the country, and especially in the province of Quebec, with the rise of the separatist movement, results from the fact that the federal government has never tried before to respect actually the use of the two official languages in Canada. It is undeniable that in all federal departments English is the only "working language".
May I mention a fact of personal knowledge. When they write to the departmental administration in Ottawa, the civil servants of the province of Quebec feel morally obliged to submit all their reports in a language other than their mother tongue.

As I already stated, it is the responsibility of the state to see to it that one of the main clauses of the confederation pact is adhered to. The federal government shall therefore have to take the required steps so that the civil servants of this country can perform their duties in their mother tongue. This problem must be tackled without delay.
In that field, the Conservative government made a worthy gesture when it introduced the latest civil service act. I am referring to section 47 which makes it an obligation for the commission to choose, in all parts of Canada, a sufficient number of bilingual civil servants to serve both major language groups.
I submit, sir, that any Canadian who wishes to make a career for himself in the civil service should consider it a duty and a moral obligation to learn the two official languages of our country.

It was in the year 1925 when the Liberal party went to the country on a program which included, among other things, the reform of the Senate.
I wish to read what was said about this in the Liberal handbook for 1925. I shall not read all of it because it would take too much of my time but I shall read the essential parts of it, if I may have the attention of hon. members. This is how it reads:
The people believe that the Canadian House of Commons should have the same power as the British House of Commons to pass legislation and the Prime Minister has personally declared this to be his view. How he is going to bring this about was fully set forth in his keynote speech in North York.

If you examine the present situation of the Canadian economy and compare it with that of other countries in Europe and America, you will find that it cannot even be compared with the one that prevailed in this country a few years ago.
The first thought that comes to mind, is to find out the causes of that stagnation and recession. Would it be that we lack resources or that we are wanting in financial and intellectual potentialities? Yet, Canada is the richest country of the world in all kinds of natural resources: lumber, coal, oil, large and numerous water courses, iron and all types of minerals, and Canadians are a healthy and hard-working people.
During the last quarter century, before the Conservatives came to power, our country made great progress and yet the means at its disposal were far from being as efficient then as those which are available nowadays. Industries have developed, means of communication have expanded and improved, the St. Lawrence has been deepened, pipe lines have been laid and numerous other services have been organized.
If Canada has known such intense development in that quarter of a century it is because we have had at the head of the government, sincere and competent men of action.

Once the elections were over, and it had secured votes from a great number of farmers because of that 1958 legislation, the government dropped the price support and replaced it by deficiency payments on very small quantities. The farmers who, in 1958, trusted the government, increased their production of pork and eggs, but in 1959, the government took away from them all the security they had been guaranteed before the elections.
What should we think of a government which, through the measures taken by its agriculture minister, brings about a continuous drop in farm incomes, thereby betraying his electoral program-

I am pleased, Mr. Speaker, to make some comments in this historic debate. I wish to make some observations regarding measures forecast in the speech from the throne. However, before proceeding to discuss various items I specifically refer to the motion before us moved by the hon. member for Laval and seconded by the hon. member for Van-couver-Kingsway. It is no mere formality so far as I am concerned when I congratulate the mover and the seconder on the subject matter of their remarks and the excellence of its presentation. I listened to the speeches with great interest and found that there were expressed by both the mover and the seconder thoughts which I consider are tremendously significant to every member, of this house, especially to those of us who are members of the Conservative party.
My friend the hon. member for Laval brought to the attention of the house the

fact that the Conservative party has always believed in private enterprise. He said private enterprise is the very essence of democracy. In his speech he stated that Canada under a Conservative regime is living its finest hours of freedom and that there is a place in the sun for everybody in this great country of ours. He stated that private enterprise and the state are two great friends who, provided they keep understanding and helping each other, will never see hovering above them the dark cloud of doubt and suspicion. And he continued, "For man is not made for the state; it is the state that is made for man". I think those eloquent words so well expressed by my friend the hon. member for Laval are most inspiring and thought provoking, and I commend them to the house for re-examination.
Then, the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway in his interesting and analytical address said much with which I concur- as a matter of fact, I usually concur with what he says anyway. However, his comments with which I find myself in complete agreement are found at page 23 of Hansard, about two thirds of the way down the first column:
The time has long passed when during the course of a single speech one could begin to recite all the accomplishments of the present administration because they are far too numerous
I think you will quite understand why I agree with those remarks. Later on, as recorded at page 27 of Hansard he made this statement which I enthusiastically endorse:
By any analysis of the government's record there is no cause for fear now or in the future. By any analysis of our economy and its future prospects there is no cause for pessimism. By any analysis whatever there is every reason for all Canadians to move forward to a greater and brighter future under the brilliant leadership of the Right Hon. John G. Diefenbaker, one of the world's outstanding leaders.
A day or two ago, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Kent, New Brunswick (Mr. Michaud), in speaking in this chamber, referred in most appropriate words to the passing of the late Senator Leger. At this time I wish to say that I subscribe fully to what he said concerning this distinguished citizen of our province. My experience with the late Senator was not as close as I would have desired it, but I always found him to be,- whether in New Brunswick or in Ottawa and under all circumstances-always the perfect gentleman. He will be greatly missed by all and I take this occasion to extend sympathy to his wife and family.
It is with pleasure that I congratulate you, sir, on having been appointed Deputy Speaker of this house. I am confident that you will

discharge your duties with all the qualities necessary to commend the respect of all hon. members and in accordance with the best traditions of this house. I am also pleased that my hon. friend, who formerly held the same position, is now the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys and I am certain that he will continue his career of distinguished public service. I am certain that he will execute his duties to the satisfaction of all concerned.
May I also express my regret at the loss I believe this house has suffered in the removal of the fine gentleman who was the immediate predecessor of the present Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys, a man of fine disposition and even temperament and a man of tremendous ability. He will bring great credit to himself and honour to our country as the representative of Her Majesty the Queen in the province of Quebec.
I should like to congratulate all who have participated in this debate. Naturally I have been more impressed by those who spoke in support of the administration than those who did otherwise. Sometimes I was rather annoyed at some of what I consider to be very undeserved criticism. However, Mr. Speaker, it has been a most interesting debate, I believe, for all concerned.
I should like at this time to say a word or two concerning the momentous event of history that took place on Tuesday, February 20, when history was made on behalf of our great friends to the south, the United States of America, by Colonel Glenn, who was the successful astronaut and space man who covered 81,000 miles, circling the earth three times and finally landing in practically the exact intended location.
I feel a distinct sense of satisfaction for myself and happiness for every citizen of the United States. Having spent the greater part of my life living practically alongside the United States border, having travelled frequently and freely back and forth, having made many friends and having acquired an addition to my family from that great country since my son brought a lovely wife with him back to Canada, I am very pleased and I rejoice with our neighbour to the south in the tremendous scientific achievement and accomplishment of Colonel Glenn on behalf of his country.
It seems to me that we in this house might very well consider that unemployment is our greatest domestic problem and, next to world peace, probably the most important one. However, I feel there is a difference between those on this side of the house and the Liberal opposition in our approach to it. We believe in and work for employment. They
The Address-Hon. H. J. Flemming seem to enjoy talking about unemployment. This has been the pattern in recent years. They never ask how the figures compare with a year ago, a month ago or how they compare percentagewise with the richest country in the world, the United States. They appear to gloat and almost express pleasure when the figures of unemployment go up, and they indicate no particular satisfaction when they go down.
I contend that the program of this government announced in the speech from the throne on November 17, 1960, has, to the extent of my knowledge, been tremendously successful. It called first of all for a larger program of assistance to municipalities for winter works. My comment is that this has been tremendously effective. Efforts have been made and are being made in every part of our country to plan our activities in such a way that there will be maximum employment during the winter season.
There is nothing new about winter unemployment. I have spent my life in the business of lumbering and in connection with woods operations we always had people employed who worked at something else during the summer. It is just that we are going through a different phase and different plans must be made in the future. There is no question, Mr. Speaker, but that the winds of change are blowing. Activities which were adequate in the past will not, for one reason or another, be adequate in the future, and it is tiding us over this period of change that renders assistance to municipalities so important since the intention is to stimulate winter works. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the winter works program was last year, is this year and will be in the future an effective program so far as meeting the problem of seasonal unemployment is concerned.
I would also draw the attention of the house to the fact that all possible public works are now being carried on during the winter season. I have no doubt, and I am sure the house has no doubt, that this will have a most beneficial effect, and it will continue to be done in the future to the fullest possible extent.
Since the employment situation is much improved this year compared with last, I wonder whether anyone has taken the trouble to ask himself or herself what has brought this about. I submit that government policy, government activity and private enterprise, inspired and assisted by government participation, are responsible for the improvement. It did not just happen.
Let me recite some of the changes instituted by the government in the past two years. We are told, Mr. Speaker, that we

The Address-Hon. H. J. Flemming need to be reminded more than we need to be educated, and so I am going to review some of the things which I think are responsible for the fact that today we have a lessening of unemployment compared with a year ago. This will continue to be the case and that should bring to every member of the house the greatest possible degree of satisfaction.
First, the government announced a five year extension of the policy of sharing in the expense of hospital construction from March, 1963, to March, 1968. I do not need to elaborate on the importance of this. I am sure that hon. members are all convinced that hospitals which are badly needed subsequent to March, 1963, will be planned for. They need to be planned for, and this program has a twofold advantage. It furnishes work and it also furnishes the hospital. Federal aid will be available and municipalities will know what they may expect in that five year period. This is most important, and the result will be more construction, more jobs, direct and indirect, and more hospitals.
There is another encouragement to construction in that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has been authorized to increase their volume and improve their terms of mortgage lending. We listened to the Minister of Public Works tell us this afternoon that Canada had the greatest record with regard to housing of any 18 million people in the world, and I submit this is due to the fact that the government has recognized the situation. We all know of the increase. We know of the great acceleration in construction generally and in the building of homes in particular. We all know that there has been a reduction in the rate charged by the corporation. We all know that this has contributed tremendously to the furnishing of employment both directly and indirectly. There is an old saying that there is no better way to improve general economic conditions than to stimulate construction, and I have no reason to doubt that that is the case today.
I should also like to draw the attention of the house to the fact that recent legislation authorized Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to become a partner with provincial authorities with respect to urban redevelopment, which is often called slum clearance, but whatever it is called it is most desirable. With respect to this action I say that it has been most definitely job producing.
Then there is the question of universities and their need for more residences. Recent

governmental action provided special authority to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to make loans for university residences on attractive terms. To my certain knowledge this has been used to a great extent by many universities.
We also have another illustration in the provision of long term loans for sewage disposal and treatment plants up to two thirds of the cost, with the special incentive that the federal government will write off, in other words, will make an outright grant of 25 per cent of the cost for all expense incurred up to March, 1963.
I should like to refer now to one item in some detail because I live in a province where waterways are tremendously important. The Saint John river, of which the upper part is international, has a difficult pollution problem, and the prevention of any increase in pollution of this waterway is vital to our province. I only cite this as one instance of the need to grapple with the situation, but to add to our difficulties so far as the Saint John river is concerned there are many branches of it flowing from the state of Maine, thus complicating an already complicated situation.
Some years ago the New Brunswick government passed legislation encouraging the municipalities to deal with the whole problem of sewage disposal and participating in the financial implications. The provincial legislation plus the federal legislation should be a tremendous incentive for all municipalities to face up to the situation, grapple with it and deal with it. I submit that this is most essential legislation. It has been used to a great extent though not to the extent it should be; but it is on the statute books, it is to the credit of the government, and in my opinion it will be of increasing value and will be recognized as such.
May I refer for a moment now to the productivity council. I do not expect to elaborate on this. It has been debated in this chamber by many members, and I am sure that the general hope and expectation are that it will bring about a great improvement. The same plan has been tried in England with outstanding results. In Canada the productivity council has become established and has held meetings. The chairman is an outstanding and successful businessman. I believe that from a long range point of view this council will achieve results and I feel we are fortunate we have so many capable people on this council rendering valuable and efficient service.
Now I have a word to say concerning guarantees for bank loans for small business, a subject which would appear to deserve

comment. As hon. members know, this measure provides for the government's guaranteeing a portion of bank loans for small businesses, to finance additions and for the improvement of business premises and equipment. A few evenings ago I listened to a debate on the floor of this chamber dealing with the extension of this act so that it might meet additional needs of something like the same general nature. Our friends in the opposition voiced tremendous concern because they said it had not been used much, in fact used so little, with only $23 million worth of applications so far. Some of them almost shed tears-I believe of the crocodile variety. Now, Mr. Speaker, I come from a part of the country where $23 million is a lot of money and when that amount of loans has been made under this general heading and realizing there has been considerable difficulty in getting a proper understanding with the chartered banks, and other difficulties which are not uncommon to new legislation, then it is my submission that properties have been improved under this legislation which otherwise would not have been improved because there was no provision under which this type of business could borrow. As a matter of fact this legislation has been an outstanding success. It has brought about increased employment and great benefit to small businesses.
Extending assistance to provincial governments for vocational training has been another one of the achievements of the government. This has led also to the retraining of those who have already become employed. The legislation likewise provides a grant of 75 per cent of the amounts expended for technical schools prior to March 31, 1963. We heard a report on this a few evenings ago from the Minister of Labour and I now have figures from him indicating that there have been 236 vocational and technical schools either built or improved under this act. The figures given me, which I believe are up to February 9, indicate that these schools will cost a total of $254,300,000, of which the federal share will be $170,000,000. I am likewise informed that of these 236 institutions 123 are new schools, 78 are additions to existing schools, and 30 are alterations to existing schools. I do not believe I need to elaborate on the importance of this assistance, or to emphasize that it has much more than one benefit because the construction of these schools furnishes a good deal of employment and stimulates employment in many industries.
Then there is the benefit in the technical education and vocational education of young people, in the opportunity furnished them to acquire a technical and vocational knowledge
The Address-Hon. H. J. Flemming so important in this age of mechanical activity and automation. I submit that this program has been a tremendous success and I believe the Minister of Labour in particular, the government in general, and the people of Canada as a whole will derive great satisfaction and benefit from this program.
Much has been said in this house concerning secondary industry, its need and its importance. I believe the house is familiar with what took place in connection with the "class or kind" legislation which was passed last year. I listened quite intently to the various debates on second reading, committee stage and third reading of that measure. In my opinion the action of certain members of the opposition, presumably with the knowledge and consent of their leader, and perhaps under his direction, gave every reason that they be accused of conducting a filibuster against this legislation. I found myself unable at that time to comprehend their attitude, and I still find myself unable to do so.
They had complained that governmental action in connection with employment was long overdue and there was nothing that might furnish, reasonably prompt amelioration of the difficult situation existing with regard to employment. They said everything was long range and that we should do something that would have an immediate impact on the unemployment situation. Yet we saw them acting in such a way that I believe would be capable of being considered obstruction, or would appear to be attempting to postpone almost indefinitely the passage of the act. I submit that when goods of a class or kind made in Canada are imported into this country, that must displace potential jobs for Canadians.
The proposed act was to give the minister authority to deal with any situation without delay. Yet we saw our friends opposite gang up in an apparent attempt to prevent the passage of that legislation. I do not know how they will explain their action to the people of Canada in the coming election. Indeed, I would not care to have the responsibility which they have. Probably they will say that eventually the act was passed, but we know what happened to it. It was not passed in the other place and consequently did not become law. In my opinion it was legislation which would have kept Canadians working at their jobs and which, in some cases, would make a direct contribution to the establishment of new jobs.
Little has been said in this house regarding the development of the Columbia river. I suppose, coming from almost the extreme eastern part of the country, it might be considered a trifle presumptuous for me to say much about it but it is a subject which
1168	HOUSE OF
The Address-Hon. H. J. Flemming is most interesting to everyone. I am sure that everyone within the sound of my voice is well aware how this matter stands at the present time. A treaty has been signed by Prime Minister Diefenbaker on behalf of Canada, and the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Finance have been working diligently and faithfully to secure agreement with the province of British Columbia.
More progress has been made under this government in connection with this great development-the greatest that Canada has ever undertaken, greater perhaps than the St. Lawrence seaway-than in any other period of our history. As a matter of fact we in the east hardly knew there was a Columbia river until the coming into office of the administration of Prime Minister Diefenbaker. I am one of those who believe that the difficulties which are now irritating, and which have brought about some delay in carrying out the plans of the government in connection with this great project and the development of this great waterway, will be overcome. I have the greatest confidence that those who are working towards a solution of the difficulties will be successful and within a short time arrangements will be made to proceed with this tremendous undertaking.
I shall now mention the program for agricultural rehabilitation and development. In connection with this objective, legislation has been passed, a director has been appointed and plans are under way whereby the aims and objects of this particular legislation will be advanced. It is a long term objective.
In the process of the establishment of the many families making up the population of this great nation undoubtedly much land has been cleared which is probably not very suitable for the growing of agricultural crops. I have no doubt that there is much cleared land in our country that is more suited to the growing of crops of trees than any other crop. I assure the house that there will be the utmost co-operation between the department over which I have the honour to preside and the Department of Agriculture, in connection with future plans under this particular legislation. Let us make no mistake about it. This is one of the most important pieces of legislation that has ever been put on the statute books of this great country.
The Minister of Agriculture has great plans for the future under this act. He is assured of complete co-operation from us and the house may be assured that I anticipate a most successful long range development under this act, all for the good of agriculture and for the good of everyone connected with it.


I wish to refer to the railway which has been mentioned by the Minister of Public Works as one of the accomplishments of the government in the carrying out of its promises. It is just within the last day or so we saw a picture in the newspapers of the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources sitting on a bulldozer. He was apparently turning the first sod for that railway. It seemed to me that this was a tremendous undertaking, 400 miles from northern Alberta into the north, the opening up of a tremendous new country and opening up great vistas and great prospects for all our people. Now we find the situation is that the funds have been voted, the survey has been completed, the work has been started and the minister drove the machine which turned the first sod. If this may be considered by the house as being a progress report, it seems to me a pretty good one. What more could we ask? For years the Liberals talked about it. We are doing it.
The speech from the throne contains many more important passages and declarations of intent. It is certainly not my purpose to try to refer to each of them because time would not permit. Hon. members will perhaps recall that I said a few moments ago in the course of these remarks that unemployment-or employment, if you like, because I prefer to refer to employment in the positive sense-that in the furnishing of employment it seems to me the peace of the world is the most important objective. The speech from the throne contains a recital of many important happenings of the past. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the preservation of peace is the most important single objective that any government could have. I refer especially to these words in the speech from the throne:
The Canadian government remains devoted to peace as its primary objective.
I see no sign of any dissent around this chamber, neither did I expect any.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to associate myself with all the previous speakers to congratulate and offer my best wishes of success to the hon. members for Quebec South (Mr. Flynn) and St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard) for the confidence the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) has shown them. I would be remiss if I did not mention the movers of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, the hon. members for Laval (Mr. Bourdages) and Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Browne). They have really shown a creative spirit in the sense that they succeeded in making something out of nothing.
The hon. member for Laval broke into the chorus his leaders have been singing since 1957 about the poor legacy left by the Liberals. Following the example set by his leaders, he voluntarily forgot, or simply ignored like his colleagues a certain part of that enviable legacy left by the former Liberal administration.
And by the way, Mr. Speaker, what was that legacy? In brief, this country lived in an atmosphere favourable to the economic expansion which had been taking place for many years; Canada still had in all parts of the world the peak of her prestige but not a peak in the sense the Conservative members from Quebec understand it; the Nobel peace prize, awarded to our former minister for external affairs, who is now the leader of the Liberal party (Mr. Pearson), confirmed the universal esteem and friendship of the countries of the world toward Canada.
To come back to the national front, the former administration, from 1946 to 1957, through an administrative policy which lent more importance to the welfare of the nation than to the welfare of the party reduced our
The Address-Mr. Loiselle public debt by almost $2J billion; there was over $900 million in the unemployment insurance fund; the former administration had also left a special fund of $165 million for national defence purposes and let us not forget the $272 million surplus in the last federal budget. Here is the true legacy left by the Liberals in 1957.
But what happened after the coming to power of a group of Conservative adventurers who were then and still are today more thirsty for domination and power than they are concerned about the general welfare of Canadians.
Here is a very concise summary of what really happened here under a Conservative administration. The conversion loan of more than $5J billion flooded the bond market, and expanding private enterprise was hard hit by those who like to call themselves its champions. The result was that Canadians will, for years and years to come, pay an additional amount of $52 million just to pay the interest on that loan. To which we must add the not inconsiderable amount of $25 million which went to pay friendly brokers' commissions as well as publicity costs. That is how the Conservatives went about upsetting our Canadian economy soon after they came into power.
In the international field, the total lack of the most elementary sense of diplomacy in some of our ministers is doing considerable damage to our good relations with Great Britain. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) himself are largely responsible for that deplorable state of affairs. Yet, they spend their time, especially the Prime Minister, posing as champions of the commonwealth. They keep talking about it, but they never miss an opportunity to undermine it. The Minister of Finance denied the reports about the speeches delivered at the Accra conference. Is it through ignorance or insincerity that he is unaware of an indiscretion of the Minister of Trade and Commerce who gave a copy of his speech to a reporter? That is how we learned the truth, the actual truth, about the almost senseless stand taken by the Canadian representatives at Accra. They pretend today that this actual truth reported in the press has been distorted and misrepresented.
The Conservatives went even further: within two years, they reduced to nothing our repayment of $2.5 billion on the public debt by increasing the debt by $2,218 million. In addition, the Conservatives have almost depleted the $900 million unemployment insurance fund, while completely draining
1170	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Loiselle the special national defence fund of $165 million as well as the $272 million surplus of the last Liberal budget. To that we must add an ever increasing number of deficits without our country experiencing in return a prosperity proportionate to its wealth. We must also take into account unemployment which again this year, and for the fourth consecutive time, has reached proportions which are truly at variance with the Prime Minister's vision of 1958. Since the opening of the session, the parrots on the government side of the house have been repeating endlessly that unemployment is less serious this year than a year ago. If that is true, the better for those who are working. However, I do not think that this will be of much comfort to the hundreds of thousands of Canadians who cannot find jobs.
That is not all. In his celestial vision, the Prime Minister had promised us a tax reduction. What happened? In the fall of 1957 and in June 1958, the Conservatives did indeed reduce taxes by an amount of $204 million. The Prime Minister promised a $500 million reduction, but to him promises are more important than deeds, as far as votes are concerned.
In the 1959 budget, the Minister of Finance raised taxes by $352 million, apart from the indirect tax on the workers, the small wage-earners in this country, as he increased by approximately $80 million the employees' and employers' contributions to the unemployment insurance fund. But that was not enough. The Prime Minister wanted to fulfil his promises to the limit. At the same time he increased the sales tax from 10 to 11 per cent as well as the tax on spirits and cigarettes and he raised from 47 to 50 per cent the tax on corporation incomes over $25,000.
Add up all those increases and you will find that the Conservatives have taken back at least two or three times the slight $204 million decrease, with the result that Canadians today pay much more in taxes than before the Conservative magicians came to power. Yet, this does not prevent the Conservative parrots from repeating, with the assurance that comes from ignorance or bad faith, that the Tory administration has reduced taxes. What reduction? The situation in which the Canadian economy really finds itself has not, by any means, prevented the specialist in sensational and resounding statements, the


Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Sevigny), from proclaiming shamelessly in Toronto, on November 4, 1960:
Never has the country been so prosperous as under the Diefenbaker administration.
Another one who, like his leader, feeds on visions.
