Mr. Speaker, I bow to your ruling, and now I would like to revert to a subject I have dealt with many times in this

house, that is the slum clearance and the provision of low rent housing. I have always been interested in that question which I have brought to the attention of the government since the Montreal St. Ann riding has elected me.
That riding is one of the oldest areas of Montreal and I must say, Mr. Speaker, that the workers who live there and that I have the honour to represent are great-hearted men who deserve consideration.
As a councillor of the city of Montreal I had the honour to be appointed to the sanitary housing board, under the previous administration. I always made it a point to emphasize the need for clearing the slums and replacing them by low rent housing.
In 1960, the sanitary housing board, asked the economic research corporation to investigate and report on the housing situation in the city of Montreal.
In the first days of July 1961, the board submitted to the present administration a very comprehensive report on the Montreal housing situation.
I may assure you, Mr. Speaker, that the report is not very encouraging and is food for thought. I would say that the report alone should have convinced our municipal board of directors and the management of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation that immediate action was imperative. To justify my statement, I shall just say that Montreal has 17,645 slum dwellings in which 29,282 families are living. Those figures mean that a total of 116,450 people, or 8 per cent of the whole population of Montreal, experience hardship in unsanitary surroundings which beggar description.
There have been people in the past who criticized the Jeanne Mance housing project. And, at this point, I want to bring to the attention of the house a financial report in this morning's Le Devoir with regard to that project, which, it is said, has yielded a surplus of $70,755.43.
Some people said, before the housing centre was built, that Montreal could not afford it. May I tell you, Mr. Speaker, that having followed closely the building of those housing units, I am very happy about the results. I am therefore pleased to point out that surplus today, as it should encourage our municipal and federal administrations to go ahead with similar projects in the city of Montreal.
The Address-Mr. Loiselle
The Jeanne Mance centre created some 800 new housing units equipped with all facilities required for modern living. Not only are there no vacant flats in those units, but I may assure hon. members that there is a waiting list which might surprise many hon. members. Even though these housing projects are not perfect, we must admit that they have made possible the clearing of an important district of Montreal and, especially, a great number of families have found in them all the comfort of a modern home. Moreover, this type of housing has greatly contributed, I am sure, to a substantial decrease in juvenile delinquency in this area. Montreal has an urgent need for several other similar housing projects, comprising units with several rooms for our large families.
In its report, the economic research corporation mentions that there are 17 blighted areas requiring redevelopment. Of these 17 residential areas, 9 were considered in a mediocre or bad condition and have been dealt with in a very detailed report.
Zones 2, 3 and 5, and a part of zones 1 and 4 are located in my constituency. May I point out, Mr. Speaker, that zone 2 covers 310 acres, zone 3, 160 acres, and zone 5, around 275 acres.
This justifies the pleas I have repeatedly put forward to the government for slum clearance and construction of low cost housing.
I therefore repeat my request to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) who is responsible for the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, and I urge him to give special consideration to the representations of the administrators of the city of Montreal, so that a favourable decision can be reached as regards assistance to these 30,000 families.
If, perchance, the minister is somewhat dubious about the merits of my statements, he might yield to my invitation and see for himself, on the spot, the conditions under which families live in these slums. I will gladly take him around. He would, therefore, be able to see for himself the inhuman and pitiful conditions under which those workers' families live in my riding. He might also have to go up or down shaky staircases.
I have here photographs which were published in Montreal newspapers showing the frightful conditions which I just mentioned. I might even draw the minister's attention to a newspaperman's caption below one of those photographs:

The Address-Mr. Loiselle
The rear balcony, which will soon give up, has many uses. It is used at the same time as a dump and as a storage for the furniture which could not be placed in the rooms of the apartment. This is where they go also if they want to get a bit of fresh air.
After a meeting in Ottawa of the mayor of Montreal with the Prime Minister (Mr. Dief-enbaker) and the Minister of Public Works, the latter, in a statement made a few days later, described Montreal as a surplus area.
I should like here to read a few sentences from an editorial published in the newspaper Le Devoir of January 19, 1961:
A peculiar situation, since Montreal may just as well be considered as a housing shortage area, because it is the only possible justification and explanation of the continued enforcement of rent control in the metropolis, 16 years after the war ended and long after all other war controls have disappeared.
Nevertheless, federal authorities are most serious in their stand for the only reason that Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is stuck with empty apartments which it cannot rent.
So we have a metropolitan area with a housing surplus and a housing shortage at the same time. There is a surplus and a wide choice for those who can afford to pay a relatively high rent and an acute shortage for those with a low income.
And the newspaperman goes on, Mr. Speaker, to explain that situation.
Again in the same connection, Mr. Speaker, I shall keep on calling the minister's attention to this very ticklish matter which is being discussed both by the Montreal authorities and by the leaders of the various organizations of the city of Montreal. In fact, I cannot but keep on renewing my representations to the minister.
As there are some hundreds of unoccupied apartments in houses built with the assistance of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the government is turning a deaf ear to the municipal authorities' repeated requests for slum clearance, to facilitate the construction of low rental housing. Such a thoroughly negative attitude on the part of the government is in no way justified, if we consider that it has granted credits for the building of housing in localities quite far from the Montreal labour centres.
In the face of the hard-headed obstinacy of the government which refuses its financial assistance for the construction of housing, the Montreal municipal authorities are considering asking the provincial government to grant them special powers to decree the freezing of municipal assessments in some areas for a ten year period.

If such a request were granted by the provincial legislative assembly, it would allow the construction of more sanitary housing, without any increase in real estate taxation during that ten year period.
However, the fact remains that those less fortunate workers are paying taxes to the federal administration and they are entitled, just as any other Canadian citizens, to benefit from the National Housing Act and from the loans granted by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. In fact, I cannot understand the obstinate attitude of the federal government towards the Montreal labour communities. The Minister of Public Works will undoubtedly allow me to appeal to his humanitarian feelings on behalf of my fellow citizens.
Mr. Speaker, I would briefly deal with another matter I raised a few times in this house. This is the construction of the C.B.C. building in the eastern part of the metropolis. Over two years have gone by since the representative of the municipal administration and those of the corporation reached an agreement on the site and purchase of land for the establishment of the whole radio and television services.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, those services are at present located in several buildings scattered throughout the city, and such a situation is very costly for the taxpayers.
The relocation of the C.B.C. services in eastern Montreal, in addition to eliminating a great many slum dwellings in an older part of the city, would be an incentive for several owners to improve their buildings. Furthermore, in many instances, we would see the construction by private enterprise of magnificent apartment blocks around that site. This would be a repetition of what is happening at present in the western part of the city along Dorchester boulevard. I am actually wondering why the government is delaying so much its decision about that project. The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) always seems to be without a definite answer in that connection. I recently put repeated questions to him and to the Minister of Public Works in an effort to obtain an encouraging answer. Unfortunately, there was nothing definite in their replies.
I ask the government to carefully examine the situation and let us know its stand on that problem which requires speedy action. Let the government say yes or no but at least let it say something sensible. If the answer is yes, I say without hesitation that the

eastern part of Montreal will be the scene of a redevelopment which is well deserved. If the answer is no, at least the municipal authorities will know where they stand.
In a transaction of this kind, the important point is not to know who gets the better part of the bargain but to be aware of any possible agreement between two governments for the sole purpose of serving the best interests of a whole community.
I hope that the Ministers of Public Works and National Revenue will be able to announce the good news shortly, so that the residents of Montreal who pay their share of taxes to the federal government may be treated fairly by those responsible in the central administration.
At this stage of my remarks, I should like to deal with a matter which is mentioned in the speech from the throne in these terms:
My government is initiating negotiations with the provincial and municipal authorities with a view to removing the tolls on the Victoria and Jacques Cartier bridges in Montreal: should these be successful you will be asked to approve legislation for this purpose.
In reply to a question which was directed to him recently, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Balcer) stated that he has had some news in connection with the negotiations going on with the province of Quebec but that he has not heard from the city of Montreal. In fact, I doubt that he will receive a definite reply from the municipal authorities of Montreal because, if my information is correct, the only exchange of correspondence between the city of Montreal and the Department of Transport is a letter marked "personal and confidential" which was sent to the municipal authorities. How then could the latter make public their views on that question when they are sent a personal and confidential letter.
Being a citizen of Montreal, I am, like my fellow citizens, in favour of the elimination of tolls on Jacques Cartier and Victoria bridges but under certain conditions, I am almost convinced that very few are aware of all the facts about the Jacques Cartier bridge and more particularly about the terms of the agreement passed between the federal, provincial and municipal governments.
As a matter of fact, according to that agreement, the city of Montreal was to pay an annual amount of $150,000 for its share of the deficits, and from 1930 to 1951 the operation of Jacques Cartier bridge cost the taxpayers of Montreal the sum of $2,789,768. From 1951 to 1957, the same operation brought financial surpluses and if my in-
The Address-Mr. Loiselle formation is correct, I believe the Quebec provincial government never paid its share of the deficits. When the authorities of the city of Montreal in 1944 decided to discontinue their payments, court procedures were initiated and, following a judgment, the city of Montreal was condemned to pay its share of the deficits for the years 1944 to 1949 inclusive. As a matter of fact it had to pay $210,407 in interest charges and $3,552 for legal fees.
Mr. Speaker, it is good politics, especially on the eve of a general election, and to save a few seats on the south shore, to offer the elimination of tolls on Jacques Cartier and Victoria bridges. I am all for it, so that my fellow citizens of Montreal might benefit from it, if possible, but provided the contract be amended and the operation of this bridge become the joint responsibility of the federal and provincial governments. Thus, the Montreal taxpayers would no longer be required to assume their share of deficits and maintenance.
The operation of the Jacques Cartier bridge, from the time it was built until now, has cost Montreal taxpayers the sum of $3,003,738. Furthermore, for the last two years, following an agreement between the federal government and the municipal administration, citizens of Montreal who have to use the Jacques Cartier bridge to get to St. Helene island, owned by the city of Montreal, have had to pay an additional amount of a little over $42,000. Why should the citizens of Montreal always be the ones to pay, when the time comes to be of service to the surrounding municipalities? It has always been said, in the past, that Montreal was the milch cow" of the surrounding municipalities.

For the last two years I have been in receipt of representations by the representatives of the Canadian boiler society protesting the importation into Canada of pressure vessels that do not meet the specifications required by the various provincial governments. Approaches have been made by the provincial chief boiler inspectors to the Departments of Trade and Commerce, National Revenue, and Finance, asking for the assistance of the federal government in controlling this problem. Thus far these approaches have met with little success, and my purpose in addressing the house today is to

lend my support to their efforts and to solicit the help of all hon. members in what I believe to be a reasonable request.
All the provinces have enacted legislation governing the manufacture, installation and operation of certain pressure vessels, the primary objective being the safety of their citizens. To this end, no boiler may be installed that does not meet the specifications set forth in that legislation. Nor may these vessels be placed in service unless they have been examined by inspectors appointed by the government for that purpose. Furthermore, no boiler may be operated except by persons who are authorized under certificate issued by the provincial department concerned, after an examination based on the type of boiler to be operated.
The number of inspectors and the task of carrying out these inspections are lessened because of the regulations governing the manufacture of boilers, and there can be no doubt that the law requiring that these boilers be built to certain specifications is the main factor responsible for the relatively few accidents due to the explosion of boilers in this country.
Adhering to these regulations does impose upon the manufacturer certain obligations which I believe they have no desire to evade, but I also believe that it is unfair to impose these requirements on Canadian manufacturers and then to allow boilers to come into Canada from foreign countries which do not impose the same requirements.
The Canadian boiler society is only asking for equal competition. If the safety of our people depends upon these boilers being built to certain specifications, then surely all boilers should be made to conform regardless of where they come from. The society has suggested that this could be brought about by the federal government requiring that all boilers imported into Canada bear a stamp indicating that they have been made according to the specifications required by Canadian regulations. As the government already requires some imports to be stamped and as there are no tariff revisions requested, there seems to be no valid reason why the suggestion made by the Canadian boiler society and the chief boiler inspectors of the provinces should not be granted, particularly as it affects the safety of Canadian citizens.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to join those who spoke before me in congratulating the hon. member for Laval (Mr. Bourdages) and the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Browne) for the excellent way they carried out their task as mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne.

I also wish to extend my congratulations to the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Flynn), the new Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys. May he also have every success in his new post, as well as the new parliamentary secretary to the Prime Minister, the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard).
At the beginning of this speech, let me say how proud I am of my chief, the leader of the Liberal party (Mr. Pearson). I listened with great attention to his speech on the address in reply to the speech from the throne and I congratulate him warmly for it. (Text):
Since September, 1960, there has been a substantial increase in the money supply. In May the government asked Mr. James B. Coyne, the governor of the Bank of Canada, to resign and since his resignation became effective there has been a startling increase in the money supply. The Coyne controversy

lasted for about four weeks and during that period there was only a moderate increase in the money supply. But in the week ending August 2 there came the largest weekly increase in the money supply that has ever taken place, $267 million. Since then there has been a further net increase of $157 million. From October, 1960, to October, 1961, the increase has been $842 million. The increase during the 12 weeks that followed the resignation of Mr. Coyne was $452 million, more than half the total year's increase.
Since the Diefenbaker government came into office there has been a great expansion in our money supply and this form of inflation, monetary inflation, can be highly dangerous. The purpose of these Diefenbaker excesses and expenses, in expanding the money supply, is no doubt to sell its bonds. The Diefenbaker government, since taking office in 1957, has had an unbroken series of deficits totalling $2,105,000,000 to March 31 last and the Minister of Finance has estimated that the deficit in the current fiscal year ending March 31, 1962, will be $980 million while the gross total up to that date will approximate $300 million, a staggering amount of money.
This cannot be accepted as a permanent way of life. The deficits should be met by direct borrowing from the public instead of by an increase in the money supply. The shocking situation which has developed as a result of this policy is that now far more Canadian assets are owned by outsiders, mainly citizens of the United States, than was the situation when this government took over in 1957. This resorting to the printing press and the new Diefenbaker dollar is bound to deliver us to foreign investors whose currencies have become so much more valuable in Canada, and we may anticipate a still larger inflow of United States and other foreign currencies, further pressure on our exchange rate, further government requirements in the capital market, further upward pressure on interest rates, and so around again in a vicious circle.

First of all, I should like to quote from an article which was published in the January 19, 1962 issue of La Presse under the signature of Mr. Vincent Prince and which reads as follows:
Once more, the government feels ostensibly generous. Let those who have been forgotten rise and be counted.

To hon. members opposite who have tried to make the people of Canada believe that the country was headed for disaster under the Conservative government, I would recommend the following subject for meditation.
In 1956, the gross national product amounted to $30.6 billion, whereas in 1961, it reached $37.4 billion. During that period, exports went up from $4.8 to $5.7 billion. Companies' profits totalled $3.55 billion in 1961, as compared with $2.91 billion in 1956. Consumer spending which was $18.8 billion in 1956 went up to $24.6 billion in 1961.
That seems at variance with the contentions of hon. members opposite that Canada is going bankrupt under the Conservatives. It will be recalled that during the 1957-58 election campaign, the Conservative party pledged itself to increase old age pensions and reduce taxes. Now, our friends opposite claim that, under the Conservatives, workers are paying more taxes than under the Liberals. I would ask you, then, Mr. Speaker, to refer to table VIII of the income tax deductions. Let us take, for instance, the unmarried worker who earned $60 a week under the Liberal regime. He paid $8.15 in personal income tax. Under a Conservative regime, he pays but $6.05.
The married worker with two children paid, under a Liberal regime, $2.93; under a Conservative regime, he pays only $2.75 in personal income tax. Those are the deductions.
Our friends opposite boast quite a lot about the prosperity we had under the previous regime, claiming that everybody had jobs and nobody suffered from unemployment. If you will but refer to figures published by the unemployment insurance commission, you will find that, from 1942 to 1956, benefits paid out amounted to the fabulous sum of $1,340,480,905.23.

speechtext:
First, I should begin by congratulating Your Honour on your appointment and saying how happy

we are to see you discharging your functions as Deputy Speaker. In addition, congratulations are due to the new Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys on his appointment.
I am sure that with our present officers we shall have a successful year. I wish, also to extend congratulations to the mover and seconder of the address on a job well done.
Canada at this time expects to continue her remarkable growth. This government and our Prime Minister have set a good example for other countries by resisting the temptation to intervene artificially to attack the problem of Canada's trade imbalance and the dollar premium while responding selectively to the needs of special areas such as those which produce textiles. All in all, it should hearten us in Canada to know that this country's outlook for the future is that of a growing economy playing a significant and responsible role in the world of trade. I am sure that all members of the house are glad to be here in, and contribute to the solution of the many difficulties which confront our country today. The purchasing power of our dollar is steady but I am positive we will weather the storm and Canada will again emerge as one of the leading nations of the world with our Prime Minister at the helm.
Of prime importance to all of us in East Kootenay, for which constituency I am speaking tonight, is the announcement that in cooperation with the United States progress is made toward the development of the Columbia river. In connection with this power project we should also include the development of the Kootenay river. The headwaters of these two mighty rivers are in my constituency. At one time a canal joined them together but only one boat went through this canal some 70 years ago. Since that time numerous studies have been made of the power potential of these two rivers. In recent years the international joint commission has finalized several plans for the development of the Columbia with a dam at Mica Creek near the northern tip of the big bend in the Columbia; also by the construction of a dam on the Kootenay at Libby mountain in the United States. This dam will back the water up into Canada for a little over 40 miles and cause many acres of farmland to be flooded. Residents in the area affected have been living in a state of uncertainty for the past 12 years, not knowing which way to turn

not knowing whether to make much needed improvement to their holdings or to make preparations to move to another location. Now it is up to our government to take action. It will mean the end of many years of waiting for those in the area, one which will eventually be under water. The construction of this dam

will mean more power available for industry-in my district, and it is my sincere wish that we will see the finalizing of this project in the near future.
Consideration should also be given to the completion of the trans-Canada highway. The northern route is now nearing completion and it is up to the government of the provinces and the federal government to complete a southern trans-Canada highway which would serve all of the southern portion of British Columbia where the greatest number of the residents of the province now work and live. Its completion will assure an expansion of the economy. This road across this section of the province-1 am still referring to the southern trans-Canada highway-will also be of great value to the present trans-Canada highway when completed by the connection road links running north and south through the province.
Up to this time we have made terriffic expenditures on the present route, which is well deserved and needed by the province of British Columbia. We also need the southern trans-Canada highway as a means to bring the tourist dollar into the thickly populated section of the province. The impact of the tourist dollar in Canada cannot be over-emphasized. Statistics show only part of the picture. The benefit to Canada and especially to our great Canadian Rockies in British Columbia is declining from lack of foresight, in not making our main highways attractive and safe for the travelling public. Leadership in encouraging the extension of the tourist season in British Columbia is essential. In my constituency of East Kootenay we have many attractions, both winter and summer, for tourists. We have good accommodation for tourists the year round.
During the past years, due to a lack of foresight on the part of the previous administration action was not taken in developing the highways that are needed in Canada today.
Going back to the period between 1930 and 1935 when we last had a Conservative administration federally, roads from the United States into Canada were classed as access roads to develop our national parks. There are portions of three great national parks in my area.
I wish to stress the need for the construction of a road from Montana through the Flathead country into the city of Fernie. We have pressed for this road both federally and provincially for many years. This road will open up not only a recreation facility but also the timber volumes which will come out of this area. It will serve to assist in fire prevention and lead to greater efforts
The Address-Mr. McFarlane in the conservation of the watershed. There is a potential in this area for gas and oil developments and the development of mineral deposits will assist the exploring companies in eastern British Columbia.
I wish also to bring to the attention of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Harkness) the need for an armoury in Kimberley where we have an active unit. Premises are being rented to carry on lectures and they are dependant on accommodation from various sources. Rental charges are high and it is not conducive to producing a good militia unit. Training suffers and administration is a problem. In our committee work we have been advised that the army would assume command in the event of a nuclear attack. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, we must have efficient and well equipped militia units and the only way this can be achieved is by supporting militia units in armouries located in active areas. The need is great in Kimberley and I am distressed when I hear that armouries are being built in areas which do not want them and we are not receiving the consideration we deserve. Thirty million dollars is budgeted this year and we are asking for a fraction of 1 per cent of this budget to construct a building suitable for our needs in Kimberley. Negotiations are now in progress with a very active committee in Kimberley who are willing to build this armoury and rent the premises to the government on a long term basis. I would like to ask the minister for his support of this project at an early date.
Consideration should be given to the question of improving airports in East Kootenay. This is of prime importance not only for the present domestic service but also in case of emergency. Present airports in the area are in need of improvement so that we can handle larger planes than those now in use. Due to physical reasons there are limitations, but I believe that improvements should be made at an early date and that this should be a federal responsibility. Millions are being spent in the larger centres and I would request the Minister of Transport to take this matter under advisement. The problem is not going to be an easy one to solve but I feel sure that the money spent would contribute to the expansion of the air services in my district.
At this time I wish to bring to the attention of the government the historical site at Fort Steele, British Columbia. The old town of Fort Steele which is about to be rehabilitated as a provincial historic site is located ten miles northeast of Cranbrook. It is set

The Address-Mr. McFarlane above a sweeping valley at the junction of Wild Horse creek and Kootenay river.
Gold was discovered on Wild Horse creek in 1864 and by midsummer a thousand miners, traders, and labourers had found their way to the new goldfield where a town sprang up. To link this new community with the coast, governor Douglas gave orders to complete the building of the Dewdney trail and by September 1865 pack trains were making the trip across British territory from Hope on the Fraser river to the Kootenay diggings.
The gold excitement was short-lived. The East Kootenay country slumbered on until it reawakened with the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway in the mid 1880's. The coming of settlers created a new situation. Fort Steele's claim to fame is that it was the first and only fort constructed and manned by the northwest mounted police in British Columbia. It saw no shooting war but acted as a deterrent to disgruntled Indians at a time that bristled with threats of violence.
The fort was built in 1887 and manned by a detachment of the northwest mounted police under the command of Colonel Samuel Ben-field Steele; hence its name. Its purpose was to intimidate insurgent Indians who felt they were being deprived of their rightful heritage of land.
This matter has been the subject of correspondence between the provincial and federal governments for some time. It was understood by the provincial government and the Cranbrook historical society that the property was to be turned over to British Columbia free of any charge. I have now been advised that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police have reported surplus a property located at Fort Steele to be acquired by the government of the province of British Columbia and converted into a park and historic site. A stone cairn and memorial bronze plaque erected on the site in 1921 and restored in 1957 recall the historic significance of the location in relation to the early days of the west and the provincial government intends to restore the site and maintain it.
The original property was obtained by the R.C.M.P. from the government of British Columbia. It included a residence for the commandant and one for the caretaker.
However, in 1955 it was deemed advisable to acquire additional land and a number of parcels were then expropriated from private owners at a cost of $3,100 to the crown in the right of Canada.
Crown Assets Disposal Corporation has offered to dispose of the property to the province for a consideration of $3,100 being

the reimbursement of the cost of the recently acquired lands, which may or may not form part of the original historic site.
The government of British Columbia wishes to acquire the entire site without charge or consideration in view of its undertaking to maintain it as an historic park and make some outlays for the restoration thereof.
I suggest that this land be turned over to the province of British Columbia for an historic site without charge and free of encumbrances. In view of the small amount involved it appears to me we could well afford to donate this land as an historic site. Development of this historic village will have great meaning to East Kootenay. Efforts are being made locally to give every assistance to the provincial officials and the historical society. Because the amount involved is small, I believe we should turn this over to the province free of charge immediately.
There are just one or two other items I should like to bring to your attention, Mr. Speaker. For a number of years the district of East Kootenay has been almost the forgotten land provincially, federally and in many other ways. There are a few conditions which I think should be brought to the attention of the government. I should like to start at the north end of the district and direct attention to the question of flooding which we run into almost every year at the present time. This valley is practically surrounded by the bend in the Columbia river at the north and by some flooding of the Kootenay river in the south. The flooding at Golden is periodic from the fact that the Kicking Horse river which runs into the Columbia brings down a great deal of waste, shale and rocks of many kinds. This causes floods in part of the valley near Golden and creates a problem for a great number of residents in that area. So far we have been unable to interest either the provincial government or the federal government-and this has been going on for a number of years- in giving us some relief in that area.
Going south in the valley we find the village of Athalmer also has a flooding condition through the fact that tributaries of creeks which become swollen in the spring bring down a great deal of refuse. In one place the water is actually running uphill into the Columbia river. A similar situation is also to be found at the village of Creston. We have a problem there also where the water coming down from the various rivers is bringing down refuse and creating a difficulty.
